REPOWER India

Affordable, reliable, clean power.
At the scale India needs.

India needs to build firm, clean power faster than any country has built it. Its existing coal sites are the quickest place to do it, but only if nuclear plants are delivered as products rather than as one-off projects.

REPOWER India

The need

India needs about 1,500 GW of firm capacity by 2050, and today it builds 0.3 GW of nuclear a year

3.2 kWh a dayIn 2023 the average Indian used 3.2 kWh of electricity a day. In the richest economies, the members of the OECD, the average was 20.7 kWh. Health and wealth depend on electricity.

13,580 TWh a yearIf every Indian used electricity at the OECD average in 2050, the grid would have to deliver 13,580 TWh a year, about eight times today's demand.

About 1,500 GW of firm capacityA least-cost hourly model of that system builds about 1,460 GW of firm capacity, generation that runs whenever it is needed, beside 1,457 GW of solar and 396 GW of batteries.

Explore all 52 weeks. The bars show generation through the year; the dashed lines mark firm capacity at 100% and its 70% operating minimum. Switch cases to make wind and solar supply about half of demand: firm capacity stays above 1,000 GW.

0.29 GW a yearIndia has added nuclear capacity at 0.29 GW a year for two decades, and never more than 1.0 GW in one year. Building 1,500 GW of firm capacity between 2030 and 2050 means commissioning 75 GW a year.

The industrial base

India has the industrial base to build at this scale

India is the world's second-largest producer of crude steel and cement. It built 10,660 km of national highway in 2024-25 and casts rail viaducts from precast girders in yards along the route. In the year to March 2026 it added 44.6 GW of solar and 6.05 GW of wind, records for both.

234 GW at 197 sitesIndia has 234 GW of coal and lignite capacity in 635 operating units at 197 sites. Each circle is a site, sized by its operating capacity. Tap a site for its details.

A young fleetMore than three-quarters of that capacity is under 20 years old. The owners hold the sites, the grid connections and the trained workforce.

US$67 per MWhIndia can also build nuclear power at a cost few countries match. Its next 700 MWe pressurised heavy water reactor (PHWR) would generate at about US$67 per MWh, one of the lowest nuclear costs in the world.

The constraints

Transmission, water and land constraints point to existing coal sites

TransmissionTo meet its 2032 transmission plan, India must add lines at 1.9 times the rate of the past four years. A coal site already has a grid connection sized for its output.

WaterOf the operating coal capacity, 64 per cent stands in sub-basins of high or extremely high water stress, where withdrawals exceed 40 per cent of the renewable supply.

LandLand acquisition for a nuclear plant takes more than four to five years. A coal site already holds land, a water allocation and a trained workforce.

The Anpara testAnpara units A, B and D in Uttar Pradesh have 2,630 MW of coal capacity. Four 700 MWe reactors, as at Gorakhpur, occupy about 6 km².

317 km²Supplying the plant's annual energy with solar power and batteries takes about 317 km², and still leaves 14 per cent of hours short.

1,114 km²Serving every hour, through the monsoon and cloud spells of three to five days, takes about 1,114 km², about 190 times the land of the nuclear station.

The coal sites

India's coal sites could supply nearly 60 per cent of the electricity needed in 2050

1,295 TWhThe operating coal fleet, 233.5 GW, generates about 1,295 TWh a year at today's load factor of 63 per cent.

389.7 GW of coal capacityAdd the units under construction, the planned units and the captive plants: 389.7 GW, or 2,160 TWh a year at today's load factor.

+912 TWhRunning all of it at a 90 per cent load factor, as a firm plant can, adds 912 TWh a year through the same connections.

+4,609 TWhHosting 2.5 times today's capacity on reconductored connections adds the rest. This is an upper limit that network studies must confirm.

7,681 of 13,580 TWhRepowered and expanded on their grid connections, India's coal sites could supply up to 7,681 TWh a year, 56.6 per cent of the 2050 need.

Nearly 60%

of the electricity India needs in 2050 could come from its existing and planned coal sites

The requirements

To compete with coal, a repowered unit must generate at US$35 to 40 per MWh and be built in a few years, not decades

A repowering product must meet eight requirements. Select a requirement to see the evidence.

    Source: Terra Praxis analysis. The end targets are programme objectives that remain to be demonstrated.

    The cost to beat: the going-forward cost of each coal unit

    A repowered unit must generate at or below the cost of keeping the coal unit it replaces running: about US$35 per MWh weighted by capacity, with unit costs from US$17.7 to US$70.7.

    The delivery models

    New delivery models could raise deployment from 0.3 GW to tens of GW a year

    0.29 GW a yearThis is India's average rate of nuclear additions over two decades.

    The fastest national programmesOver their 20-year build periods the United States added 4.3 GW of nuclear a year, France 2.9 GW and China 2.7 GW. Even those rates fall short of the need.

    Products, not projectsFaster rates need the reactor to become a product made in a shipyard or a factory rather than a project built on site. Private capital is already funding these models.

    Two to three factories: up to 75 GW a yearAt 20 to 25 GW a year per factory, two to three factories could deliver 40 to 75 GW a year. The new bar shows how scaling to three factories could reach India's need of 62 to 75 GW a year.

    This is illustrative capacity at sustained output: two factories alone would deliver 40 to 50 GW a year.

    The product

    REPOWER turns a nuclear plant into a product for coal sites

    REPOWER is a delivery model designed against these requirements, and it does not depend on a new reactor. A seismically isolated standard building, and thermal storage between the reactor and the steam cycle, make the plant independent of the site. A configurable kit of parts, made in factories and assembled on site, applies design for manufacture and assembly (DfMA). The delivery model can change in four stages without changing the reactor.

    Source: Terra Praxis analysis based on LucidCatalyst for Urenco (2025), MoSPI (2024), GEM (2026), Kang and Petrunik (2003), NPCIL (2014) and CIMSEC.

    Design for manufacture and assembly

    On day 436 the yard-precast unit is ready for equipment, while today's method is still building its containment wall

    A Terra Praxis schedule model of one 700 MWe PHWR, on the geometry of Kakrapar 3 and 4, tests how far precast and modular construction could shorten the civil works. Scroll to run the clock. The three cases build the same twin-unit station.

    Day 0

    Model plan values built on analogues; no Indian precast nuclear cycle has been measured. Day 0 is the start of the unit-1 raft. Unit 1 at right with a quarter cut away; unit 2 at left. Source: Terra Praxis PHWR 3D model, steps S3 and S4 (October 2026).

    Day 0: the first raftAll three cases build the same twin-unit station. Day 0 is the start of the unit-1 raft. Ground works start half a year earlier in the precast cases and a year earlier in today's method.

    Yard-made parts arriveOrange parts are finished in a casting yard beside the site; amber parts are yard-made shells filled on site. Grey is cast in place.

    Day 340: fully modular is readyThe fully modular case has finished its containment wall and is ready for equipment. Its yard makes 48 per cent of the concrete.

    Day 436: yard precast is readyWith 38 per cent of the concrete made in the yard, the precast case is ready for equipment. Today's method is still building its containment wall.

    Day 675: today's method is readyWith 22 per cent of the concrete made in the yard, today's method reaches the same point 335 days later than fully modular.

    The outer domesBy the time today's method closes the outer dome of unit 1, both precast stations have long finished their containment structures.

    Fully modular construction could finish the outer dome 761 days earlier

    The cost

    Reusing coal sites and building as a product could bring a 700 MWe PHWR to about US$44 per MWh

    US$67 per MWh todayThe next 700 MWe PHWR, built in eight years and financed at 10 per cent, would generate at about US$67 per MWh. Financing is the largest part.

    US$48 as a seriesBuilt as the nth of a kind, in six years at 8 per cent, with lower capital and operating costs, the same plant comes to about US$48 per MWh.

    US$44 on a coal siteReusing the infrastructure of a coal site lowers the capital cost by a further 20 per cent: about US$44 per MWh.

    Below US$40, indicativeA factory-made 50 MWe fast reactor could come slightly below US$40 per MWh. This is an indicative case for a later phase.

    The acceleration programme

    A five-action acceleration programme can start now, with the coal units that nuclear power would undercut

    The first action is to screen the coal sites. A coal unit is a candidate where keeping it running costs more than a new nuclear unit would. Choose a nuclear cost to see which units qualify.

    At US$70: no clusterAt a nuclear cost of US$70 per MWh only three units qualify, 0.6 GW. There is no cluster at all.

    At US$60: 10.9 GWAt US$60 per MWh, 45 units qualify, 10.9 GW. The first clusters form.

    At US$50: 30.7 GWOf these, 13.1 GW are units older than 20 years, the reference case for repowering.

    At US$40: 57.0 GWAt US$40 per MWh, 209 units qualify and form large clusters across the country; 18.7 GW of all qualifying capacity is in units older than 20 years.

    The other four actions

    • Pre-license sites, so that site studies and approvals are complete before a project is awarded, as India's Central Electricity Authority has already proposed.
    • License one, build many. The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board would approve a design once under the final regulations of India's 2025 nuclear energy law and review each site for conformity with it.
    • Use digital tools. Terra Praxis has tested its site platform against 13 coal sites with 24 GW in Ukraine.
    • Design for manufacture and assembly. China's first two Canadian-designed heavy water reactors were built in under five years, and the model above shows how far factories could go.

    The first 36 months

    Existing Indian institutions can own almost every action

    Months 1 to 6: screen the sites and settle the rules

    The Central Electricity Authority and the Nuclear Power Corporation of India screen the coal sites and publish a named list. The Authority and the state governments hold grid connections and water allocations for successor units. The Department of Atomic Energy and the Nuclear Power Corporation settle the rules under the 2025 nuclear energy law, the tariff and lifetime fuel and heavy-water contracts before bids open.

    Months 7 to 18: prepare the sites and structure the first orders

    The Nuclear Power Corporation, the Central Electricity Authority and the host states form a company to prepare the listed sites. The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board defines the site envelope and lets one design approval serve successive sites. Indian industry helps standardise the design before the first order.

    Months 19 to 36: order the fleets and invest to scale

    The national generator and the state generating companies order identical units in fleets. Industry builds precast and module capacity sized to a firm order book, and lenders price the lower risk of a standard design into the cost of capital.

    India built most of its coal fleet in two decades. Its sites, connections and people can carry the next build-out.

    Repowering them is the fastest place to start. The full report sets out the requirements, the evidence for each one and the 36-month programme.
